stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Marine biologists once assumed that a whale carcass sinking to the deep-sea floor was a brief feast, stripped bare within a few months and then abandoned. Observations of such "whale falls," however, have revealed a far longer sequence. Hagfish and sleeper sharks do remove most of the soft tissue during the first year. Snails, crabs, and worms then crowd into the enriched sediment around the skeleton for up to two years more. Finally, bacteria digest the oils stored in the bones, releasing sulfide compounds that feed mussels and clams, sometimes for half a century.
choices: To argue that scavengers remove less of a whale carcass's soft tissue than biologists assumed
To describe the succession of communities that a sunken whale carcass can support for decades
To illustrate how bacteria in whale bones release compounds that feed deep-sea mussels and clams
To explain why biologists expected sunken whale carcasses to be stripped bare within months
explanation: First, find what every sentence has in common. The opening gives the old view, that a whale carcass is a short feast. The 'however' sentence says there is actually a longer sequence. The last three sentences go through that sequence in order: scavengers in the first year, then snails, crabs, and worms for up to two more years, then bacteria, mussels, and clams for as long as fifty years. Each sentence adds a stage, and together they show that one carcass supports a series of different communities over decades. The text only reports observations and never makes an argument, so 'describe' is the right verb. Choice B is the only option that covers the whole text.

A.why: You noticed that the text corrects an old belief, which is the right first step, but you assumed the wrong part of that belief was being corrected. The text says scavengers 'do remove most of the soft tissue,' so it confirms that part of the old view. What it corrects is how long the carcass keeps supporting life, not how much the scavengers eat.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. Everything in this choice is true, but it only covers the last sentence, the final stage. The scavengers and the sediment-dwelling animals before it are left out, so this is one detail, not the purpose of the whole text.

D.why: The text states the old assumption in its first sentence but never says why biologists held it. No reasons are given, so the text can't be explaining them. You picked a choice built on the opening line and expanded it into something the text doesn't do.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Immunologists have traditionally divided the immune system into two branches: an adaptive branch that remembers specific pathogens and an innate branch that responds the same way to every threat. Yet innate cells, it turns out, can be primed by experience. Monocytes taken from people months after they received the BCG tuberculosis vaccine release more inflammatory signaling molecules when exposed to unrelated fungi and bacteria. The change traces to the bone marrow, where the vaccine alters how tightly DNA is packaged in the stem cells that produce new monocytes. Researchers call this nonspecific, long-lasting priming "trained immunity."
choices: To explain how the BCG vaccine changes DNA packaging in stem cells within the bone marrow
To argue that innate cells remember particular pathogens much as adaptive cells do
To propose that the BCG vaccine be given to protect people against fungal infections
To describe a lasting but nonspecific priming in the branch long thought to lack memory
explanation: Track the structure. The text starts with the traditional view that only the adaptive branch has memory and the innate branch always responds the same way. 'Yet' then introduces a phenomenon: innate cells can be primed. The next sentences give an example (BCG-exposed monocytes react more strongly to unrelated microbes) and a mechanism (changes in the bone marrow), and the last sentence names the phenomenon and calls it 'nonspecific' and 'long-lasting.' Every sentence is there to present trained immunity, and the text informs rather than argues. Choice D covers the whole text and keeps the detail that the priming is nonspecific.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. The DNA-packaging mechanism really is in the text, but it is one supporting sentence. The text uses it to explain where the phenomenon comes from, not as its main subject. This choice leaves out the traditional view, the monocyte evidence, and the naming of trained immunity.

B.why: You correctly saw that the text revises the old view of the innate branch, and then took that revision too far. The text says the priming works against 'unrelated' microbes and calls it 'nonspecific.' Innate cells are not shown remembering particular pathogens the way adaptive cells do, which is the difference the text is careful to keep.

C.why: The text reports that BCG-exposed monocytes react more strongly to fungi, but it never recommends using the vaccine against fungal infections. 'Propose' needs an explicit recommendation, and this text only describes findings.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Economists have often described union hiring halls, where dockworkers once gathered each morning to be assigned shifts, as inefficient holdovers that slowed the matching of workers to jobs. Labor historian Inés Calderón's study of the hall at the Port of Tamsen complicates that picture. Assignment ledgers from 1952 to 1971 show that the hall rotated shifts by seniority within skill grades, so that crane operators rarely waited more than a day for work, and that ships unloaded there turned around faster, on average, than those at nearby nonunion piers.
choices: To show that union hiring halls were, as a rule, more efficient than the arrangements economists preferred
To present evidence from one port that challenges a common view of how a labor institution performed
To explain the seniority system that one port's hiring hall used to assign shifts to crane operators
To trace how economists came to see union hiring halls as holdovers that slowed the matching of workers
explanation: The text opens with a common view (hiring halls were inefficient), says Calderón's study 'complicates that picture,' and then gives ledger evidence from a single port. Every sentence serves that purpose: one port's records push back on a widely held view. The verb 'challenges' matches the text's 'complicates,' and 'from one port' keeps the claim as narrow as the evidence.

A.why: You spotted the correction, which is the key insight, and then stretched it further than the text does. The evidence comes from one port, and the text never says what economists preferred. 'As a rule' turns one case study into a general law.

C.why: The seniority rotation really is in the text, but it is only one piece of the evidence. This choice leaves out the faster turnaround times and, more importantly, the view that the evidence challenges.

D.why: Only the first sentence is about the economists' view, and the text never traces how that view developed. This choice describes the setup and misses the evidence that makes up most of the passage.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Seismometers are expensive to install on the seafloor, so the ocean bottom is poorly monitored. Geophysicist Tomás Reyna has found a substitute already lying in place: the fiber-optic cables that carry internet traffic between continents. When a seismic wave stretches a cable, it slightly alters how laser pulses scatter inside the glass, and those alterations can be read as a record of ground motion every few meters along the line. Infrastructure built for one purpose can quietly serve another. Using a single 40-kilometer cable off Chile, Reyna's team detected hundreds of small offshore earthquakes that land stations had missed.
choices: To argue that fiber-optic cables should replace seismometers on the seafloor
To explain why seismometers have been difficult to place on the seafloor
To describe a method that uses existing undersea cables to record earthquakes
To claim that most infrastructure could be adapted to serve scientific research
explanation: Each sentence fits under one heading: what the method is (cables as sensors), how it works (laser scattering), and what it achieved (hundreds of earthquakes detected). The text informs rather than argues, so the neutral verb 'describe' fits, and 'existing undersea cables' covers the whole account.

A.why: The word 'substitute' pulled you toward a recommendation the text never makes. The text says the cables can stand in where seismometers are scarce. It does not say they should replace seismometers, and 'argue' needs an opinion that isn't there.

B.why: The cost of seismometers is the opening background, given only to explain why a substitute matters. One clause of setup can't be the purpose of the whole text.

D.why: You noticed the one abstract sentence, which was a good thing to notice, and then treated it as the thesis and inflated it. The text says infrastructure 'can' serve another purpose, not that 'most' of it could. That sentence is a side comment on Reyna's method, not the point the passage builds toward.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: In the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, western hemlocks often stand in straight rows, their roots arching over empty space. Each row marks where a fallen tree once lay: seedlings sprouted on the rotting trunk, and when it decayed, the young trees were left standing on stilts. Ecologists call such trunks nurse logs. Why seedlings favor them was long unclear, but ecologist Mara Lindqvist found that seedlings planted on bare forest floor survived well when moss was cleared away, suggesting that logs help mainly by raising seedlings above smothering moss.
choices: To describe a forest pattern and present a finding about what causes it
To explain how the roots of some hemlocks come to arch over empty space
To show that rotting logs give seedlings nutrients the forest floor lacks
To argue that clearing moss from forests would improve tree regeneration
explanation: The text first describes a pattern (rows of hemlocks on stilts, grown from nurse logs). It then raises an open question (why do seedlings favor logs?) and answers it with Lindqvist's finding (logs lift seedlings above the moss). The right purpose has to cover both halves.

B.why: The text does explain the stilt roots, but only in its second sentence. This choice covers the opening and leaves out the question and the study that take up the second half.

C.why: The name 'nurse log' suggests nourishment, but the study points the other way. Seedlings did well on bare ground once the moss was gone, so the benefit is height, not nutrients.

D.why: The finding is about why seedlings survive on logs, and the text recommends nothing. 'Argue' and a forest-management proposal go well past an explanation of one natural pattern.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: When the Orrin Street Viaduct opened in 1928, newspapers celebrated its length: at 1.4 kilometers, it was the longest concrete span in the region. As engineering historian Lena Okafor notes, however, the viaduct's lasting influence came from something few visitors noticed. Its designer, Ruth Calloway, divided the deck into short segments separated by joints packed with tarred felt, allowing the concrete to swell and shrink with the seasons without cracking. Within a decade, the approach had become standard on bridges across the country.
choices: To report the length that made the viaduct the longest concrete span in its region
To argue that newspapers praised the viaduct for a feature engineers thought trivial
To explain how felt-packed joints let concrete swell and shrink without cracking
To describe a bridge and point to an overlooked feature behind its influence
explanation: The text turns on 'however.' The bridge's famous feature (its length) is set aside for the feature that actually made it influential (the segmented deck and its joints), and the last sentence confirms that influence. The right choice names both the bridge and the overlooked feature.

A.why: The length is the setup that the 'however' turns away from. You picked a true detail from the first sentence instead of the point the text moves to.

B.why: You caught the contrast, but the text never says engineers thought the length was trivial or that the newspapers were wrong. It says the bridge's lasting influence came from elsewhere. 'Argue' and 'trivial' make that contrast harsher than the text does.

C.why: This is how the joints work, which is one sentence of the passage. It leaves out the viaduct, the contrast with its fame, and the influence that is the reason the joints are mentioned at all.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Most surviving records of eighteenth-century weaving were kept by mill owners, who noted output and wages but rarely the cloth itself. The pattern book of Agnes Muir, a handloom weaver in Paisley, Scotland, is a rare exception. Across 212 pages, Muir pasted a snippet of every cloth she wove beside the threading draft used to produce it, and she annotated failures as carefully as successes. A craft's knowledge often survives only where a practitioner chose to write it down. Historians now use Muir's book to reconstruct techniques that no mill ledger describes.
choices: To claim that craft knowledge survives only when practitioners write it down
To present a weaver's record and explain why it matters to historians of the craft
To describe how one weaver arranged cloth samples alongside her threading drafts
To argue that mill owners deliberately left weavers' techniques out of their records
explanation: The text sets out a gap (mill records ignore the cloth), introduces Muir's book as the exception, describes what the book contains, and ends with how historians use it. 'Present' a record and 'explain why it matters' covers each of those steps.

A.why: You picked out the one general sentence, but you changed its 'often' to 'only' and treated it as the main claim. In the passage it is a comment on Muir's book, not the claim the book is offered to support.

C.why: The text does say how the samples and drafts were arranged, but that is a description of the book's contents. It leaves out why the book matters, which the first and last sentences make the point.

D.why: The text says mill owners 'rarely' recorded the cloth. It says nothing about why. 'Deliberately' adds a motive, and 'argue' adds an accusation, and neither is in the text.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For decades, archivists catalogued Henrik Dahl's 1868 map of the Vessa delta as an unfinished draft. Many of its channels are drawn only in dotted lines, and several islands appear twice, in slightly different positions. A reexamination by cartographic historian Priya Natarajan suggests the map is complete. Comparing it with Dahl's field notes, she found that the dotted channels hold water only during spring floods and that the doubled islands mark where sandbars stood in summer and in winter. Dahl, it appears, mapped a landscape that would not stay still.
choices: To present a reinterpretation of a map's odd features as a record of seasonal change
To criticize archivists for carelessly cataloguing a complete map as an unfinished draft
To explain why the sandbars of a river delta shifted position between summer and winter
To urge that other maps catalogued as drafts be reexamined using surveyors' field notes
explanation: The text starts with an old belief (the map was unfinished), names the features behind that belief (dotted channels, doubled islands), and then gives Natarajan's correction: those features record seasonal change. The verb 'present' fits the text's measured tone ('suggests,' 'it appears').

B.why: You saw that the archivists were wrong, which is right, but the text never blames them. Being mistaken isn't the same as being careless, and 'criticize' needs an opinion that the text's neutral tone doesn't show.

C.why: The text says that the sandbars moved with the seasons, not why they did. The movement is the explanation for the map's features, not the subject of the passage.

D.why: The text deals with one map and makes no recommendation. Turning one reexamination into a call to review other maps adds a prescription the passage never makes.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Hydrologists have long known that a stream's flow rises after rain, but it has been unclear how much of that rise is new rainwater and how much is older groundwater pushed out by it. Hydrologist Daniel Osei set out to test this in a small Welsh catchment. Because rain and groundwater carry slightly different ratios of oxygen isotopes, he could track each source in the stream. During storms, he found, more than two-thirds of the water in the channel had been underground for weeks before the rain fell.
choices: To explain how oxygen isotopes distinguish rainwater from groundwater in streams
To argue that rainfall has little effect on the amount of water a stream carries
To show that in all catchments, storm water in streams is mostly old groundwater
To report a finding about where the water that swells a stream during storms comes from
explanation: The text poses a question (is storm flow new rain or old groundwater?), describes how Osei tested it, and gives the answer (mostly old groundwater). 'Report a finding about where the water comes from' covers the question, the method and the result without saying more than the single study shows.

A.why: The isotope method is only how the question was answered, and it takes up one sentence. This choice leaves out the question and the result.

B.why: Once you see that most storm water is old, it's tempting to conclude that rain doesn't matter. But the text starts by saying flow rises after rain. The rain still causes the rise; it does so by pushing out groundwater.

C.why: You read the result correctly, then spread it to 'all catchments.' Osei studied one small catchment in Wales, so the text can't support a universal claim.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Divers have long regarded the pistol shrimp as little more than a source of noise: the snap of its oversized claw, loud enough to interfere with sonar, crackles across warm reefs. Marine biologist Keiko Arai has documented a less obvious side of the animal. The shrimp dig burrows in reef sediment and share them with gobies, small fish that watch for predators while the nearly blind shrimp maintain the tunnels. In Arai's survey plots, the burrows also aerated sediment to a depth of half a meter, sustaining worms and clams that sheltered there.
choices: To explain how the pistol shrimp's claw makes a snap loud enough to disrupt sonar
To describe the partnership in which gobies stand guard while shrimp dig tunnels
To present overlooked ways in which an animal known for its noise supports reef life
To argue that the pistol shrimp does more good than harm to the reefs it inhabits
explanation: The text sets up the common view (the shrimp is mostly a noise), then turns to 'a less obvious side' and gives two examples: the shared burrows with gobies, and burrows that aerate sediment for worms and clams. 'Overlooked ways' covers both examples, and 'present' matches the informational tone.

A.why: The snap belongs to the old view that the text moves away from, and the text never explains how the claw produces it. You fixed on the first sentence.

B.why: The goby partnership is real and in the text, but it is only the first of two examples. The choice leaves out the aeration finding and the contrast with the shrimp's reputation, so it is too narrow.

D.why: You saw the shift from nuisance to benefit, then turned it into a verdict. The text never compares the shrimp's harms with its benefits, and the word 'argue' needs an opinion the text doesn't state.
